The groups G_{k,1} of Richard Thompson and Graham Higman can be generalized in a natural way to monoids, that we call M_{k,1}, and to inverse monoids, called Inv_{k,1}; this is done by simply generalizing bijections to partial functions or partial injective functions. The monoids M_{k,1} have connections with circuit complexity (studied in another paper). Here we prove that M_{k,1} and Inv_{k,1} are congruence-simple for all k. Their Green relations J and D are characterized: M_{k,1} and Inv_{k,1} are J-0-simple, and they have k-1 non-zero D-classes. They are submonoids of the multiplicative part of the Cuntz algebra O_k. They are finitely generated, and their word problem over any finite generating set is in P. Their word problem is coNP-complete over certain infinite generating sets.   Changes in this version: Section 4 has been thoroughly revised, and errors have been corrected; however, the main results of Section 4 do not change. Sections 1, 2, and 3 are unchanged, except for the proof of Theorem 2.3, which was incomplete; a complete proof was published in the Appendix of reference [6], and is also given here.

Moreover, they are submonoids of the multiplicative part of the Cuntz algebra \(\mathcal{O}_k\). They are finitely generated, and their word problem over any finite generating set lies in \(\mathrm{P}\); over certain infinite generating sets, their word problem is coNP-complete.

The Thompson–Higman groups \(G_{k,1}\) admit natural generalizations in terms of partial functions. Allowing arbitrary partial functions yields the monoids \(M_{k,1}\), while restricting to partial injective functions produces the inverse monoids \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\).

For every \(k\), both \(M_{k,1}\) and \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\) have strong structural properties: they are congruence-simple and \(J\)-0-simple, and each has exactly \(k-1\) nonzero \(D\)-classes. Moreover, both families are finitely generated and can be realized as submonoids of the multiplicative part of the Cuntz algebra \(\mathcal{O}_k\).

Their algorithmic behavior depends on the choice of generators. With respect to any finite generating set, the word problem for these monoids is solvable in polynomial time. By contrast, for certain infinite generating sets, the word problem becomes coNP-complete.

The Thompson–Higman groups \(G_{k,1}\) can be described through bijections between finitely generated essential right ideals of the free monoid \(A^{*}\), where \(A\) is an alphabet of \(k\ge 2\) letters. This work extends that construction by allowing more general maps. Replacing bijections by partial functions yields the monoids \(M_{k,1}\), while restricting to partial injective functions yields the inverse monoids \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\). Elements are represented by right-ideal morphisms and identified through maximal essential extensions, so that the original group \(G_{k,1}\) appears naturally as the group of units. In developing these generalizations, the work also revises a number of earlier arguments and corrects errors in previous proofs.

The resulting monoids have strong structural properties. Both \(M_{k,1}\) and \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\) are finitely generated and congruence-simple. They are also \(J\)-0-simple: apart from the zero element, all elements belong to a single \(J\)-class. Their finer Green-relation structure consists of exactly \(k-1\) nonzero \(D\)-classes, distinguished by an invariant related to the cardinalities of the finite prefix codes that generate the relevant right ideals, taken modulo \(k-1\). These results place the monoids among highly homogeneous algebraic structures while also revealing a finite internal stratification not visible at the level of \(J\)-classes.

The paper further connects these monoids with operator algebras. Using the standard generators of the Cuntz algebra \(O_k\), right-ideal morphisms can be represented inside its multiplicative structure. This gives embeddings of \(M_{k,1}\) and \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\) into the multiplicative monoid of \(O_k\), extending the familiar relationship between Thompson–Higman groups and Cuntz algebras.

Finally, the work investigates the complexity of the word problem. For every fixed finite generating set, the word problems of these monoids are decidable in deterministic polynomial time. The complexity changes when certain natural infinite generating sets are used, however: in that setting, the word problem becomes coNP-complete. Thus the study not only generalizes the Thompson–Higman groups algebraically, but also clarifies how representation choices affect the computational difficulty of equality. Together, the structural, operator-algebraic, and complexity results establish \(M_{k,1}\) and \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\) as natural and significant monoid analogues of the groups \(G_{k,1}\).

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main algebraic and computational complexity results concerning \(M_{k,1}\) and \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\), including Green relations, congruence simplicity, finite generation, and word problems.
counterfactuals.output:
For every \(k\ge 2\), the Thompson–Higman monoid \(M_{k,1}\) consists of maximal essential extensions of right-ideal morphisms of \(A_k^*\); \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\) is its inverse submonoid of injective elements.

- **Green relations.**
  - In \(M_{k,1}\), the \(\mathcal R\)-class of an element is determined by its image right ideal, up to essential equality, while its \(\mathcal L\)-class is determined by its kernel congruence, again up to essential equality.
  - In \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\), these specialize to the usual inverse-monoid description: \(\mathcal L\) is determined by the domain and \(\mathcal R\) by the image, modulo essential equality.
  - Apart from \(0\), the monoids are \(\mathcal J\)-simple: all nonzero elements lie in one \(\mathcal J\)-class.
  - Their nonzero \(\mathcal D\)-classes are indexed by the size of an image code modulo \(k-1\). Thus there are exactly \(k-1\) nonzero \(\mathcal D\)-classes. The maximal subgroups include the Thompson–Higman groups \(G_{k,1}\), with related maximal subgroups occurring in the other \(\mathcal D\)-classes.

- **Congruence simplicity.**  
  Both \(M_{k,1}\) and \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\) are congruence-simple: every congruence is either equality or the universal congruence. This is stronger than their nonzero \(\mathcal J\)-simplicity and shows that they have no proper nontrivial quotient monoids.

- **Finite generation.**  
  Both families are finitely generated for every \(k\ge2\). Their generating sets can be built from generators of \(G_{k,1}\), together with a small number of elementary partial maps; for \(M_{k,1}\), one additionally needs a noninjective “merging” map.

- **Word problems.**
  - With respect to any fixed finite generating set, the ordinary word problems of \(M_{k,1}\) and \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\) are decidable in polynomial time.
  - For the natural circuit-like generating sets—generators of \(G_{k,1}\) augmented by indexed adjacent transpositions (“wire swaps”)—the word problems become **coNP-complete**. Equality of two monoid elements corresponds to equivalence of the Boolean-like partial transformations they compute; inequivalence has a short witness, which gives membership in coNP, while circuit-equivalence reductions give hardness.
  - Thus the complexity depends strongly on representation: finite-generator words admit polynomial-time algorithms, whereas succinct, circuit-style descriptions yield coNP-completeness.

Overall, \(M_{k,1}\) and \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\) combine strong simplicity properties and a very explicit Green-structure with finite generation, while their computational behavior ranges from polynomial-time word problems to coNP-complete succinct word problems.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an arXiv-style abstract for a paper that generalizes the Richard Thompson–Graham Higman groups \(G_{k,1}\) to monoids and inverse monoids, and append a “Changes in this version” note.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract.** We introduce monoid and inverse-monoid analogues of the Richard Thompson–Graham Higman groups \(G_{k,1}\), for \(k\ge 2\). The constructions are based on maximal essential extensions of finitely generated right-ideal morphisms of the free monoid \(A^{*}\), where \(|A|=k\). The resulting monoids \(M_{k,1}\) and \(\operatorname{Inv}_{k,1}\) contain \(G_{k,1}\) as their group of units and extend the familiar representation of \(G_{k,1}\) by finite prefix-code tables. We develop their basic algebraic structure, including normal forms, finite generation, Green relations, and natural partial orders, and compare the monoid, inverse-monoid, and group settings. These constructions provide a common framework for studying Thompson–Higman type symmetries when maps are allowed to be noninvertible or partially defined, and connect the resulting algebraic questions with finite-state and circuit-like computation.

**Changes in this version.** We have clarified the definitions of essential restriction and maximal extension, expanded the comparison between \(M_{k,1}\), \(\operatorname{Inv}_{k,1}\), and \(G_{k,1}\), corrected several minor errors, and improved the presentation of the structural results.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: What results are proved about the monoids \(M_{k,1}\) and \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\), their relationship to the Cuntz algebra \(\mathcal O_k\), and the complexity of their word problems?
counterfactuals.output:
For every \(k\ge 2\), the main results are:

- **Algebraic structure.**  
  \(M_{k,1}\) is the monoid of maximally extended homomorphisms between finitely generated right ideals of \(A_k^*\), while \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\) is its inverse submonoid consisting of the injective maps. Both are finitely generated and congruence-simple. Their common group of units is the Thompson–Higman group \(G_{k,1}\).

- **Realization inside the Cuntz algebra.**  
  If an element is represented by a table
  \[
  p_iw\longmapsto q_iw,
  \]
  it is represented in \(\mathcal O_k\) by
  \[
  \sum_i S_{q_i}S_{p_i}^{*},
  \]
  where \(S_1,\dots,S_k\) are the canonical Cuntz isometries. The Cuntz relation
  \[
  \sum_{a\in A_k}S_aS_a^*=1
  \]
  exactly reflects the elementary expansion/maximal-extension operation on tables. This gives a faithful monoid representation of \(M_{k,1}\) in the multiplicative monoid of \(\mathcal O_k\). Elements of \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\) correspond to partial isometries, and elements of \(G_{k,1}\) to unitaries. The complex linear span of these table elements contains the usual algebraic Cuntz algebra and is dense in \(\mathcal O_k\).

- **Word-problem complexity.**
  - With respect to any fixed finite generating set, the word problems of \(M_{k,1}\) and \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\) are decidable in polynomial time.
  - With respect to the natural **circuit-like generating set**, obtained by adjoining the position transpositions
    \(\tau_{i,i+1}\), their word problems are **coNP-complete** under the standard weighted encoding.
  
  The hardness comes from the ability of these generators to simulate Boolean or reversible circuits; equality of monoid elements then captures circuit equivalence. Thus the same monoids have polynomial-time word problems under ordinary finite-generator metrics but coNP-complete word problems under the circuit-oriented encoding.
